title: 7 small changes that help melatonin work better
summary: Timing, light and what you eat after 8pm all change how well a low dose works. Here’s what our doctors tell patients first.
body:
Melatonin isn’t a sleeping pill. It’s a signal. A low dose tells your body clock that night has started, and how well that signal lands depends a lot on what else you do in the evening.

Why timing matters

Your body starts releasing melatonin about two hours before your usual bedtime. Taking a gummy right as you get into bed means it’s working against the clock instead of with it.

“If you can only change one thing, change the timing. Most patients who say melatonin doesn’t work are taking it too late.”

1. Take it 45 minutes early

Set a reminder for 45 minutes before you want to be asleep. If your bedtime is 22:30, take it around 21:45.

2. Dim the lights at 9pm

Bright overhead light, especially cool white LEDs, slows your natural melatonin. Switch to lamps and warm bulbs for the last hour.

3. Keep your phone out of bed

Charge it across the room. Scrolling keeps your brain alert long after the screen goes dark.

4. Eat dinner earlier

A heavy meal late at night keeps your body busy digesting. Aim to finish eating at least three hours before bed.

5. Keep the room cool

Your body temperature drops as you fall asleep. A cool, dark room (around 24°C with the AC) makes that easier.

6. Same bedtime, even on weekends

Shifting bedtime by two hours on Saturday is like flying to another time zone. Keep it within an hour if you can.

7. Know when to ask for help

If you’ve had trouble sleeping for more than three weeks, or you snore loudly and wake up exhausted, talk to a doctor in person. These can be signs of conditions melatonin won’t fix.

title: How to beat jet lag on a Jakarta to Tokyo flight
summary: Tokyo is two hours ahead of Jakarta. A small shift, but enough to cost you the first night. Here’s how to land on local time.
body:
Tokyo is two hours ahead of Jakarta. It sounds small, but an overnight flight plus a two-hour jump is enough to leave you wide awake at midnight and foggy at your 9am meeting.

Start shifting two days before

Go to bed and wake up 30 to 60 minutes earlier for the two nights before you fly. Your body clock moves about an hour a day, so a head start means less to catch up on arrival.

Sleep on the plane only if it’s night in Tokyo

On a red-eye, try to sleep for most of the flight: eye mask, earplugs, no screens. On a day flight, stay awake and save sleep for local bedtime.

“Light is the strongest signal your body clock gets. Use it on purpose: bright light in the morning at your destination, dim light in the evening.”

Get morning light on day one

Spend 20 to 30 minutes outside before 10am local time. It tells your brain the day has started and pulls your clock forward.

Use a low dose at local bedtime

If you use melatonin, take a low dose around 30 to 60 minutes before local bedtime for the first few nights. More isn’t better: a higher dose can leave you groggy the next morning.

Keep caffeine to the morning

Coffee after 2pm local time can push your first night’s sleep even later. Switch to water or decaf in the afternoon.

Coming home

Flying west is usually easier. Stay up until a normal Jakarta bedtime and get morning light the next day.

title: Why your brain gets loud at bedtime, and what helps
summary: The moment the lights go off, the to-do list starts. Here’s why that happens and a few ways to quiet it.
body:
All day your attention is busy with work, messages and noise. When you finally lie down in a quiet, dark room, the thoughts you pushed aside have space to come back. That’s why worries often feel loudest at bedtime.

Give your thoughts somewhere else to go

Keep a notebook by the bed. An hour before sleep, write down tomorrow’s to-do list and anything on your mind. Getting it on paper tells your brain it doesn’t need to hold on to it overnight.

Build a buffer before bed

Stop work and stressful conversations at least an hour before you want to sleep. Swap them for something calm and repetitive: a shower, stretching, a book, a cup of caffeine-free tea.

“Your mind needs a runway to land. If you go from emails straight to the pillow, it’s still flying.”

Try slow breathing

Breathe in through your nose for four counts and out for six. Longer out-breaths help your body move from alert to rest. Five minutes is enough to notice a difference.

Don’t fight it in bed

If you’re still awake and restless after about 20 minutes, get up, keep the lights low and do something quiet until you feel sleepy. Lying there frustrated teaches your brain that bed is a place to worry.

When to talk to someone

If racing thoughts, low mood or anxiety keep you up most nights for more than a few weeks, talk to a doctor. Ongoing worry deserves real support, not just a better routine.

title: Waking up at 3am? Here’s what’s usually behind it
summary: Waking in the middle of the night is common. Staying awake for an hour isn’t. Here are the usual causes and what to try.
body:
Everyone wakes up briefly a few times a night, usually without remembering it. The problem starts when you wake fully around 3am and can’t get back to sleep.

Common causes

Alcohol. A drink can help you fall asleep, but as it wears off a few hours later, sleep becomes lighter and broken.

A warm room. Your body temperature rises slightly in the second half of the night. A room that’s too warm makes it easier to wake.

Stress. Stress hormones naturally start rising in the early morning. If you’re under pressure, that rise can wake you up.

Late caffeine. Caffeine stays in your body for many hours. An afternoon coffee can still be working at 3am.

“Don’t check the clock. Seeing ‘3:12’ starts the countdown in your head, and that’s what keeps you awake.”

What to try

Keep the bedroom cool and dark, move your last coffee before 2pm and keep alcohol to earlier in the evening. If you wake up, keep the lights off and your phone away, and try slow breathing. If you’re still awake after about 20 minutes, get up and do something quiet in dim light until you feel sleepy again.

When to see a doctor

If you wake up gasping or choking, snore loudly, need to urinate many times a night, or wake up most nights for more than three weeks, see a doctor. These can point to conditions that need proper treatment.

title: Melatonin, chamomile and L-theanine: what each one does
summary: Three ingredients, three different jobs. Here’s how each one fits into a better night.
body:
The ingredients in sleep supplements aren’t interchangeable. Each one works in a different way, which is why the right choice depends on what’s keeping you up.

Melatonin: the timing signal

Melatonin is a hormone your body makes in the evening to signal that night has started. A low dose taken at the right time can help you fall asleep sooner, especially when your body clock is off, like after travel or shift work. It isn’t a sedative, so more isn’t better.

Magnesium: support for staying asleep

Magnesium glycinate is a gentle, well-absorbed form of magnesium. It’s often paired with melatonin for people who fall asleep fine but wake up during the night.

L-theanine: calm without drowsiness

L-theanine is an amino acid found in tea. It’s used to support a calm, relaxed state, which can help when a busy mind is what keeps you up. It doesn’t make you feel sleepy on its own.

Chamomile: a traditional wind-down

Chamomile has been used for generations as part of an evening routine. It’s a gentle option for people who prefer to avoid melatonin.

“Match the ingredient to the problem. Trouble falling asleep, waking at night and a racing mind are three different issues.”

Before you start

Talk to a doctor before taking any sleep supplement if you’re pregnant or breastfeeding, under 18, take other medication or have a long-term health condition. Our assessment checks these for you.

title: The 30-minute wind-down routine our doctors recommend
summary: A simple routine for the half hour before bed. No supplements needed.
body:
Your body doesn’t switch from busy to asleep in a second. A short, repeatable routine gives it time to shift gears, and after a week or two the routine itself becomes a signal that sleep is coming.

30 minutes before bed: lights down

Turn off overhead lights and use lamps with warm bulbs. Put your phone on charge outside the bedroom or across the room.

25 minutes: get ready for bed

Brush your teeth, wash your face, change into sleep clothes. A warm shower can help, since the drop in body temperature afterwards supports sleepiness.

15 minutes: empty your head

Write down tomorrow’s to-do list and anything that’s on your mind. Close the notebook.

“Do the same steps in the same order every night. Consistency matters more than which steps you choose.”

10 minutes: something slow

Read a paper book, stretch gently or listen to calm music. Avoid anything with a cliffhanger.

5 minutes: breathe

In bed with the lights off, breathe in for four counts and out for six. Let your body feel heavy.

Make it stick

Keep the same bedtime, even on weekends. If a routine doesn’t help after a few weeks of trying, or you have trouble sleeping most nights, talk to a doctor.
